title: The Samaritan woman (John 4:1–26)
hook: a well, a thirsty Jew, a woman with five husbands, and worship in spirit and truth

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bridegroom's friend, glad to fade: he must increase. Your line was this my joy is fulfilled.

Midday, by the usual reading of John's clock. A well outside a Samaritan town called Sychar, and a tired man sitting on its edge, alone; his friends have gone to buy food. "Jesus therefore, being wearied with his journey, sat thus on the well: and it was about the sixth hour." A woman comes with her jar. And the tired man, a Jewish teacher in Samaritan country, does something she doesn't expect. He asks her for a drink.

She's surprised: "How is it that thou, being a Jew, askest drink of me, which am a woman of Samaria? for the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans." They were neighbors divided over where God should be worshiped, as she'll say herself: our fathers worshiped on this mountain, and you say Jerusalem. Jesus answers with a riddle. If you knew who was asking, you'd have asked him, and he'd have given you living water. Some readers point out that living water could also mean plain running water, and she takes him literally: you have nothing to draw with, and the well is deep. Then he turns to her life. Go, call your husband. I have no husband. True, he says: you've had five, and the man you're with now isn't your husband. Some preachers have called her a sinner. The text never says why she had five husbands. Widowhood, divorce, something else: John is silent, and some readers now hear more loss than scandal. She doesn't run. She asks which mountain is the right one. And Jesus says an hour is coming when it won't be this mountain or Jerusalem. "God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth." Then he says plainly who he is: "I that speak unto thee am he." He says it to a Samaritan woman whose name John never gives. This week: a fig tree, the best wine last, a temple that's a body, wind, God so loving the world, a friend glad to fade, and now a well at noon.
screen: then, large: `IN SPIRIT AND IN TRUTH.`

segments.voice: Wherever you are is the well: a kitchen, a car, a bench, nothing holy about it in the usual way. Let two words sit with you: spirit, what's alive in you under the noise, and truth, one honest thing about your life you'd usually leave out. If you pray, bring both to God just as they are, right here; if you don't, simply be honest and awake for these minutes.
Living water, what Jesus offers an unnamed woman at the well, who takes it at first for plain water from a spring.
Your line: in spirit and in truth. A well at noon, and a question about mountains. Another week on the path.

howItsDone: Some lectionaries set this story in Lent; the Orthodox Church honors the woman as Saint Photini, and her conversation is used to teach that worship isn't bound to one place.

original.note: Greek: living water. the phrase could also mean fresh running water from a spring, and she hears it that way.

chat.says: Why does the woman at the well matter so much? Wasn't she just a sinner?
options: The text never says why she had five husbands, and Jesus told her plainly who he was.
She was the first to recognize Jesus right away, without asking him a single question.
Jesus told her the Samaritan mountain was the right place to worship after all.
chat.meaning: John is silent on why she had five husbands, and it's to her that Jesus says plainly: I that speak unto thee am he.

Sychar.meaning: a Samaritan town near the well

Samaritan.meaning: from Samaria; neighbors divided from Jews over where to worship

living water.meaning: Jesus's gift; also a phrase for running water

notes: Index carry 'in spirit and in truth' matches KJV 4:24.
Claim that this is Jesus's longest recorded conversation in John: widely stated; confirm against Nicodemus (3:1–21) and the Farewell Discourse (which is largely monologue).

Claim that John 4:26 is the first time in John that Jesus plainly says who he is: removed from voice in review (debated; cf. 1:51, 3:13–14); 'longest conversation' softened to 'many readers count' in voice, word and myth. Confirm.
'Living water' as an idiom for running/spring water: standard in commentaries. Confirm.
Reading of the five husbands as possible loss rather than scandal is presented as 'some readers'. Confirm fair balance.
Orthodox tradition names her Photini; confirm for howItsDone.
